content: 1. Methenamine and hyoscyamine should be administered orally as one tablet or capsule every six hours, accompanied by liberal fluid intake. This combination therapy is only to be used after a urinary tract infection (UTI) has been eradicated using appropriate antibiotics. 2. Methenamine is indicated for the prophylaxis or suppression of chronic, recurrent UTIs when long-term therapy is required. 3. Hyoscyamine is used as an adjunctive treatment for lower urinary tract hypermotility and spasm. Its safety and efficacy have not been established in patients under 16 years of age. For patients aged 16 years or older, the recommended dose is one tablet or capsule orally every six hours with liberal fluid intake, and it should only be used after UTI eradication with other antibiotics. 4. Hyoscyamine should be avoided except in short-term situations to reduce secretions due to its high incidence of anticholinergic effects, as noted in the Beers criteria. 5. Glucagon increases the toxicity of hyoscyamine through additive effects on gastrointestinal motility inhibition. Co-administration of anticholinergic drugs and glucagon increases the risk of gastrointestinal adverse reactions. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 6. Glycopyrronium tosylate (topical) and hyoscyamine may enhance each other’s effects due to pharmacodynamic synergism, leading to additive anticholinergic adverse effects. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 7. Pramlintide and hyoscyamine exhibit pharmacodynamic synergism, resulting in synergistic inhibition of gastrointestinal motility. This combination is contraindicated. 8. Revefenacin and hyoscyamine both decrease cholinergic effects or transmission, potentially causing additive anticholinergic effects. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 9. Hyoscyamine decreases the effects of secretin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Concomitant use of anticholinergic drugs may cause a hyporesponse to secretin stimulation testing. Discontinue anticholinergic drugs at least five half-lives before administering secretin. 10. Sofpironium (topical) and hyoscyamine may result in additive anticholinergic adverse effects due to pharmacodynamic synergism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 11. Hyoscyamine and umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol (inhaled) may increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, leading to additive anticholinergic adverse effects. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 12. Hyoscyamine increases the effects of abobotulinumtoxinA through pharmacodynamic synergism. Drugs with anticholinergic effects may potentiate botulinum toxin effects, resulting in excessive neuromuscular weakness and heightened systemic anticholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor. 13. Hyoscyamine and aclidinium both decrease cholinergic effects or transmission. Use caution and monitor. 14. Hyoscyamine and amantadine may increase anticholinergic adverse effects due to pharmacodynamic synergism. Use caution and monitor. 15. Hyoscyamine and amitriptyline both decrease cholinergic effects or transmission. Use caution and monitor. 16. Hyoscyamine and amoxapine both decrease cholinergic effects or transmission. Use caution and monitor. 17. Anticholinergic/sedative combinations and hyoscyamine both decrease cholinergic effects or transmission. Use caution and monitor. 18. Hyoscyamine decreases the levels of aripiprazole by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Aripiprazole increases the effects of hyoscyamine through pharmacodynamic synergism. Use caution and monitor for additive anticholinergic effects and possible hypoglycemia. 19. Benztropine and hyoscyamine both decrease cholinergic effects or transmission. Use caution and monitor for additive anticholinergic adverse effects. 24. Bethanechol increases cholinergic effects, while hyoscyamine decreases them. The effect of this interaction is unclear. Use caution and monitor. 25. Buprenorphine (long-acting injection) increases the effects of hyoscyamine through pharmacodynamic synergism. Co-administration may increase the risk of urinary retention and/or severe constipation, potentially leading to paralytic ileus. Use caution and monitor. 26. Hyoscyamine and levodopa may interact in complex ways. Anticholinergic agents may enhance the therapeutic effects of levodopa but can also exacerbate tardive dyskinesia. At high dosages, anticholinergics may decrease the effects of levodopa by delaying its gastrointestinal absorption. Use caution and monitor. 62. Co-administration of olanzapine and other drugs with anticholinergic activity can increase the risk for severe gastrointestinal adverse reactions related to hypomotility. Use caution and monitor. 73. Hyoscyamine increases the toxicity of oliceridine by increasing the risk of urinary retention and/or severe constipation, which may lead to paralytic ileus. Monitor for signs of urinary retention or reduced gastric motility if oliceridine is co-administered with anticholinergics. 74.
